source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Skilled intuition needs two things: an environment with valid, learnable cues, and enough chance to practice and learn those cues. If either is missing, a correct intuition is luck.
numbers: Two conditions. Chess masters estimated at about 10,000 hours; a child needs few examples to tell dogs from cats. Validity is defined as causal and statistical structure of the environment, not as absence of uncertainty.
quote: Without these opportunities to learn, a valid intuition can only be due to a lucky accident or to magic
limits: Position paper by two rival camps, not an experiment. Validity is judged by argument and examples, with no scale to measure it. Talent and deliberate practice also matter (they cite Ericsson).
agent_relevance: The gate for a fast answer should ask two questions: is this task class regular, and has the agent had feedback on it? A fluent answer alone is not evidence.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Expertise is fractionated inside a profession. Shanteau 1992 lists fields with good expert performance (livestock judges, astronomers, test pilots, soil judges, chess masters, physicists, accountants, grain inspectors, photo interpreters, insurance analysts) and fields with poor performance (stockbrokers, clinical psychologists, psychiatrists, admissions officers, court judges, personnel selectors, intelligence analysts).
numbers: Nurses, physicians and auditors appear on both lists. Task features that separate the lists: predictable outcomes, amount of experience, good feedback, static (not dynamic) stimuli. Weather forecasters do better on temperature and rain than on hail.
limits: Shanteau 1992 is cited, not read by us. The lists rest on reviews and reputation, not one dataset.
agent_relevance: Trust must be set per task class, not per agent. The same agent can be reliable on one sub-type and not on another, so the track record must be kept per class.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Subjective confidence is not a reliable sign of validity. It follows how consistent the story is, not how good the evidence is, so redundant weak evidence yields high confidence. The safe test is the validity of the environment plus the judge's history of learning it.
numbers: Cites Einhorn & Hogarth 1978, Griffin & Tversky 1992, Arkes 2001. First impulse is usually right and usually correctable, but checking is effortful System 2 work that people skip.
quote: The safe way to evaluate the probable accuracy of a judgment ... is by considering the validity of the environment
limits: The confidence-accuracy link is described as not consistently high, not as zero. The cited studies were not reopened.
agent_relevance: Do not use the model's own stated or felt certainty as the gate. Use outcome history for the task class. Self-reports can be a weak extra signal only.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Some environments cannot yield skill (long-range political forecasting) and some are wicked (regularities exist but mislead). High validity does not mean no uncertainty: poker and bridge count as high validity because skill raises the hit rate without guaranteeing wins.
numbers: Tetlock 2005: after 15 years, experts were not better than newspaper readers on long-term political forecasts. Hogarth's wicked example: a physician who palpated tongues to confirm typhoid hunches and spread infection, so the intuitions confirmed themselves.
limits: Whether an environment is valid is often unknown in advance; Tetlock's result was a surprise to the field. The wicked case is an anecdote.
agent_relevance: Self-fulfilling feedback is a trap: if the agent's own action shapes the outcome label, the track record is inflated. Record must come from independent ground truth.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009), reporting Goldberg (1970) and Karelaia & Hogarth (2008)
finding: Human judges are noisy. Models of the judge, fit by regression to the judge's own past calls, beat the judge on new cases. That points to inconsistency as the main cause, not missing insight.
numbers: Goldberg 1970: 29 clinicians, psychotic vs neurotic, 861 patients, 11 MMPI scales; bootstrap models almost always more accurate than the clinicians they modeled. Karelaia & Hogarth 2008 meta-analysis said to confirm the effect is general.
limits: Second-hand: original Goldberg and Karelaia papers not opened. Bootstrapping beating the judge does not show the judge has no valid cues.
agent_relevance: Consistency is a cheap lever: sample several times and aggregate, or fit a simple rule to the agent's own past valid calls. Both remove noise without adding knowledge.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: The two camps agree on the rule: trust fast judgment when the environment is regular and the judge has had learning chances; distrust it otherwise. The disagreement came from which cases each camp had in mind.
numbers: Meehl 1954 reviewed about 20 studies of judges vs simple models. Kahneman in the Israeli army: officer-candidate assessments had negligible validity per later feedback, yet felt conviction did not shrink (illusion of validity).
limits: The agreement is the two authors' joint position reached through chosen examples. The paper has no head-to-head experiment.
agent_relevance: The agent should first test which regime it is in, then choose fast or slow. The rule is about the regime, not about the mechanism.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Inside a domain with real experts there are still new situations. A mark of authentic expertise is noticing that a case is anomalous. Weak ability to separate right from wrong intuitions is the norm, though pattern-violation detection (typicality, familiarity) works.
numbers: Physicians meet diagnoses new to them; weather forecasters worse on hail than on routine weather; chess is nearly unique in having no truly new challenges.
limits: Descriptive argument. No numbers on how well anomaly detection works.
agent_relevance: A novelty check on the input is a valid trigger to leave fast mode: if the case is far from the task-class record, deliberate.

source: Kuncel, Klieger, Connelly & Ones (2013) Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions decisions: a meta-analysis
finding: Across work and school criteria, a formula combining the same data beat holistic expert judgment, by a large margin for job performance.
numbers: Mean validity mechanical vs clinical: job performance .44 vs .28; advancement .42 vs .36; training .31 vs .16; GPA .58 vs .48; three non-grade academic outcomes .47 vs .46 (clinical side only 161 students). For job performance the gain is more than 50% in prediction.
limits: Population-level estimates (Hunter-Schmidt barebones, shrinkage for multiple R). With the strictest new-sample shrinkage the mechanical edge vanished but did not reverse on two criteria. No correction for criterion unreliability or range restriction, so likely an underestimate.
agent_relevance: Where a validated formula exists, let it combine the agent's feature ratings instead of a holistic final answer. The agent is better as a feature rater than as an integrator.

source: Kuncel, Klieger, Connelly & Ones (2013) Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions decisions: a meta-analysis
finding: The gap held although judges knew the job and organization and often had more information than the formula. The authors reject three usual defenses of clinical judgment.
numbers: About 25% fewer correct hires with holistic combination at selection ratio .30 (Taylor-Russell). Defenses answered: changing jobs (no evidence; job dimensions stable; linear models robust to weight changes, Dawes 1979), small samples (use meta-analytic or pooled expert weights), and expert-set weights in a formula still beat the clinician.
limits: The authors argue that clinicians do not adapt to change; this is not tested directly. Selection is a low-validity environment by the Kahneman-Klein standard.
agent_relevance: Familiarity and extra information did not rescue the holistic judge. More context in the prompt is no reason to skip a structured combination step.

source: Aegisdottir et al. (2006) The Meta-Analysis of Clinical Judgment Project: fifty-six years of research on clinical versus statistical prediction
finding: Mental health practitioners were modestly less accurate than statistical methods. The effect is small in the cleanest subset.
numbers: Search screened over 35,000 articles, coded 4,617, 1,135 met project inclusion; this meta used 67 studies and 92 effect sizes. Strict set (cross-validated formulas, outliers removed): 41 studies, 48 effects, d+ = .12 (r+ = .06), homogeneous Q(47)=65.83, CI above zero. Of 48 effects: 25 (52%) favored statistics, 18 (38%) no difference, 5 (10%) favored clinicians. 99 further null studies needed to cancel the effect.
limits: 12 of 60 effects (20%) dropped as outliers to get homogeneity; with outliers kept, heterogeneity was significant. Judges were mental health professionals and trainees across 11 task types.
agent_relevance: The advantage is real but small (about 0.12 SD). A statistical combiner is a safe default, not a sure win; per-task checks still matter.

source: Aegisdottir et al. (2006) The Meta-Analysis of Clinical Judgment Project: fifty-six years of research on clinical versus statistical prediction (moderators)
finding: Moderators did not follow the familiarity story. Clinicians did relatively better on unfamiliar data than on data from their own setting. Linear formulas beat clinicians; hand-built logical rules did not.
numbers: Data setting: clinicians from same setting as data d+=.14, not from same setting d+=.06 (QB(1)=6.96, p<.01). Formula type QB(3)=11.94, p<.01: linear .15, logical rules .03 (CI includes zero). Clinician expertness QB=2.47, not significant. Task type QB=12.42, p<.05 (brain impairment .05, offense or violence .17, hospital stay .02).
limits: Many cells are tiny (n of 1 to 5) and some appear only in parentheses. Heterogeneity remained inside some classes.
agent_relevance: Experience in a setting did not close the gap to a formula. A track record must be measured against a baseline, since felt familiarity misleads.

source: Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz & Nelson (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis (abstract and citing papers)
finding: Mechanical prediction was about 10 percentage points more accurate. Clinicians were substantially better in only 6-16% of studies. The advantage held across tasks, judge types, experience levels and data types; clinicians did worse when interview data were used.
numbers: About 136 studies (secondary sources only). Mechanical clearly better in 33-47% of studies. d = .12 as quoted in Aegisdottir 2006 and in a 2024 geopolitical-forecasting review.
limits: We read only the abstract text from a search result and citing papers, not the paper. Study count is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Same direction as Kuncel 2013 and Aegisdottir 2006, and it adds that experience level did not moderate.

source: Tutorial on mechanical decision-making for personnel and educational selection (open access, authors not recorded)
finding: Mechanical combination matches or beats holistic combination, yet practitioners seldom use it. The tutorial shows unit-weight and category-sum rules that need no large data, and names practical limits.
numbers: Example: Apgar score, 0-2 on five dimensions (cited via Kahneman 2011). Methods called fast and frugal; with large databases, regression or relative-weights analysis is better. Coarse categories lose information.
limits: Only the abstract, intro and discussion text were checked. Tutorial, not new data.
agent_relevance: A usable design: the agent rates cues, a fixed small rule adds them. Works for task classes with little data and is auditable.

source: Human and algorithmic predictions in geopolitical forecasting: quantifying uncertainty in hard-to-quantify domains (2024, authors not recorded)
finding: Geopolitical forecasting is algorithm-unfriendly, so humans stay in charge, but algorithms help as aggregators, variance-splitters and hybrids. Hybrids were mostly untested in the old clinical-vs-statistical debate.
numbers: Quotes Grove 2000 d = .12 across psychology, medicine, forensics, finance. Best predictors of forecaster skill: frequent incremental belief updating, granular use of the probability scale, logical coherence, intersubjective accuracy.
limits: Review; claims about hybrids come from tournaments, not a head-to-head trial.
agent_relevance: Hybrids of agent judgment plus aggregation fit the scaffold. Skill signals (updating, granularity, coherence) can be logged per task class.

source: Tetlock, Mellers, Rohrbaugh & Chen (2014) Forecasting tournaments: tools for increasing transparency and improving the quality of debate
finding: In a government-run tournament with over 200 questions, the Good Judgment Project beat the crowd average using training, teaming, selection of top forecasters and better aggregation. Selected top forecasters did not regress to the mean.
numbers: Best aggregates right side of 50/50 on 86.2% of daily forecasts; beat the control group (alone, no training) by 60% and other teams by 40% on Brier score. Drivers: recruitment about 10% of advantage; debiasing training about 10% over no training; teaming or markets about 10% over solo; aggregation tuning added about 35% over unweighted mean. Top 2% per year formed 5 teams of 12 in year 2 and beat year-4 goals.
limits: Reported by the winning team. Experts predicted regression; the data contradicted them. Questions were short-term, not the long-range kind Tetlock 2005 found impossible.
agent_relevance: Skill in a hard environment can be found and kept when feedback is fast and scored. The agent needs scored feedback to build its own record.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters (abstract only)
finding: Top performers kept their accuracy across hundreds of questions and many topics. Four overlapping explanations: abilities and styles, task-specific skills, motivation, enriched environments.
numbers: Elite teams drawn from yearly top performers; no regression reported (abstract level).
limits: Only the abstract was seen via search. A 2025 Psychological Science reanalysis (snippet only) reports the ability-to-accuracy link changed after controlling extraneous variables.
agent_relevance: Persistent skill is real but partly context-bound; check track records for method confounds.

source: Katsagounos, Thomakos, Litsiou & Nikolopoulos (2021) Superforecasting reality check: evidence from a small pool of experts and expedited identification
finding: A smaller and faster replication supports the idea that superforecasters can be identified, and finds preliminary benefit from 20 minutes of training on structured analogies. Evidence for the second question was weaker.
numbers: 314 initial experts; 9-month identification phase. Top 25% bin: males 24.2% vs females 11.3% (chi2(1)=4.808, p<.05); 16-20 years of experience 40%.
limits: Authors say evidence for RQ2 was much less and held only over the whole distribution. Small sample; profile effects are post hoc; different questions than GJP.
agent_relevance: Skill selection works with small pools, but demographic and experience patterns are noisy and should not be turned into rules.

source: Residents' time to diagnose and diagnostic accuracy: a randomized within-subjects experiment (2021, BMC Medical Education, PMC8061054)
finding: Slowing down is not shown to improve diagnosis. Within the same residents, correct diagnoses were reached faster than incorrect ones, and they were held with more confidence.
numbers: 117 internal medicine residents, multi-center; 113 analysed. Availability-bias induction failed (no significant effect). Correct 115 s vs incorrect 129 s, t(112)=4.51, p<.001, d=0.37. Confidence correct vs incorrect d=0.89; perceived complexity d=0.67; effort d=0.81. Bias-error trend: 115 s vs other errors 136 s, p=.082.
limits: Failed bias induction means no test of the bias claim itself. Case difficulty can explain part of the speed gap, which the authors reject mainly because confidence-accuracy calibration was poor and help requests did not track accuracy.
agent_relevance: Instructing a model to 'think longer' has weak support as a general fix. Easy cases are fast and right; the hard question is telling which cases are easy.

source: Same paper (PMC8061054), background on earlier studies by Sherbino, Norman and Meyer
finding: Earlier studies found faster diagnoses were as often or more often correct than slower ones, and that clinicians' confidence and wish to ask for help did not reflect their accuracy.
numbers: Sherbino et al. and Norman et al. were between-subjects; Meyer et al. measured confidence and help-request intent against accuracy. No figures were given in the citing paper.
limits: Second-hand; the original papers were not opened. Between-subjects design lets better clinicians be the fast ones.
agent_relevance: Confidence and self-requested help are weak triggers to escalate. Use record-based triggers.

source: A 'blip of knowledge' study: metacognition and diagnostic decision-making (2026, Cognitive Research, PMC12988131)
finding: Brief exposure to medical knowledge produced the worst accuracy and the most overconfidence, and overconfident people sought less new information. The result is on lay participants, not experts.
numbers: Experiment 1: Short-knowledge condition less accurate than No-knowledge and Long-knowledge by 0.09 each (p<.05); no stage effect. Experiment 2 (N=86; 30 no, 27 short, 29 long knowledge): no accuracy differences; overconfidence tied to choosing not to seek more information.
limits: Lay participants and symptom vignettes; Experiment 2 did not replicate the accuracy gap of Experiment 1. Not about professional intuition.
agent_relevance: Partial knowledge is the dangerous state for confidence. An agent with a little related experience may feel more sure than its record warrants.

source: Aggadi, Coon, Kibbey & Busey (2026) More skilled, more cautious: expertise and decision thresholds in fingerprint examination (PMC13683028)
finding: In two large black-box datasets, examiners with higher discriminability (d') set more conservative thresholds for same-source calls. Exclusion thresholds were not related to skill. Personality showed no relation.
numbers: Two datasets: Latent Print Black Box 2 and Kibbey et al. Signal-detection model with multiple criteria. Effect found for identification threshold, not exclusion threshold. Exact sample sizes not recorded.
limits: Observational; pre-publication date near today. Variability arises from both sensitivity and threshold, so error rates mix two causes.
agent_relevance: In a regular, feedback-rich task, skill shows up as calibrated thresholds. The agent can treat its own decision threshold as something to tune from record, separate from accuracy.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false items when formatted right. They can judge P(True) of their own samples, and a trained P(IK) predicts whether they know an answer. Calibration of P(IK) fails on new tasks.
numbers: Seeing many own T=1 samples improves P(True). P(IK) trained on TriviaQA: out-of-distribution calibration often quite poor, models mostly underconfident. RLHF policies looked miscalibrated but a temperature change fixed it. 'None of the above' option reduces accuracy and calibration.
limits: Anthropic models of that time. Calibration needs the right format and in-distribution training; shift breaks it.
agent_relevance: Self-assessed trust works inside a task class it was calibrated on and degrades on new classes. This supports a per-class record plus a novelty check.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
finding: Agreement among sampled answers correlates highly with accuracy, so low agreement signals low confidence. It lets the model 'know when it doesn't know'.
numbers: Consistency (share of decodes agreeing with the final answer) is highly correlated with accuracy on GSM8K (Figure 5). Footnote: the language model is not well calibrated on its own and cannot separate correct from wrong solutions by itself.
limits: Works only where the final answer can be compared across samples. Cost grows with samples. Correlation not a guarantee.
agent_relevance: Sample agreement is a cheap validity signal for a first answer: accept when samples agree, deliberate when they split.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without an outside correctness label, asking a model to review and fix its first answer did not help and often hurt. Earlier gains came from using the true label to stop.
numbers: With oracle labels GPT-3.5/GPT-4: GSM8K 75.9->84.3 and 95.5->97.5; CommonSenseQA 75.8->89.7 and 82.0->85.5; HotpotQA 26.0->29.0 and 49.0->59.0. Intrinsic self-correction round 2 (5 calls): GPT-3.5 GSM8K 74.7, CSQA 41.8, HotpotQA 25.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 89.0 (from 95.5), CSQA 80.0, HotpotQA 43.0 (from 49.0).
limits: Few models and benchmarks; prompts follow earlier papers. Authors also find multi-agent debate no better than self-consistency at equal responses, and that some past gains came from weak initial prompts.
agent_relevance: Deliberation by the same model, with no new information, is not a safe fallback for a distrusted first answer. Escalation needs an external check, tool or new evidence.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute
finding: On built tasks, longer reasoning made accuracy worse. Five failure modes: distraction by irrelevant detail (Claude), overfit to problem framing (OpenAI o-series), drift from sensible priors to spurious features, trouble tracking constraints in deduction, and amplified concerning behaviors.
numbers: Four task families: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features (500 students; zero-, 8-, 16-shot), deduction, AI-risk. Grades regression, zero-shot: controlled overthinking showed consistent inverse scaling for Claude Sonnet 3.7, Claude Opus 4 and o3-mini; Qwen3-32B scaled positively; others partial or flat; natural overthinking was mostly noisy or flat, clear only for Sonnet 3.7 and o3-mini.
limits: Tasks were built to expose the failure, so rates are not typical. Patterns differ by model, so not a universal law.
agent_relevance: More thinking is not free: on some task classes a longer chain makes the first answer worse. The right amount of deliberation is a per-class property to be measured.

source: Meehl lecture slides revisited by Recht, 'Clinical versus statistical prediction'
finding: The clinical-vs-statistical comparison is fair only for well-posed questions with a small set of outcomes, a fixed data set and machine-readable data. Early evidence: Burgess 1928 (psychiatrists lost to a crude rule for recidivism) and Sarbin 1943 (a clerk matched trained clinicians).
numbers: No new numbers; the slides restate Meehl 1954 and cite Allport 1942 and Bradford Hill 1952 on whether individuals are unique.
limits: Teaching slides, not a primary source; the year is approximate.
agent_relevance: The comparison that favors formulas needs a fixed, well-posed task with measurable outcomes. For open-ended tasks the evidence does not apply directly.
